justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with only modest drift upward across horizons. For the 1-day estimate, I anchored heavily on recent price levels and short-term momentum, assuming mean-reverting behavior around the prevailing range with minimal overnight catalyst risk. The 1-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild upward bias that could come from gradual trend continuation or positioning dynamics, while the 1-month estimate extends that drift further, incorporating a slightly more optimistic structural view while acknowledging that the longer horizon introduces compounding uncertainty about direction.

The confidence interval widths were deliberately calibrated to widen progressively across time horizons, which reflects standard uncertainty scaling with time. For the 1-day window, the tight interval assumes relatively low intraday volatility and absence of major scheduled catalysts. By the 1-week horizon, macro data releases, central bank commentary, or sector-specific news can materially shift prices, so the interval expands accordingly. At 1 month, the range becomes quite wide because a full month contains multiple potential regime-shifting events — earnings cycles, inflation prints, geopolitical developments — each of which could independently reprice the asset by several percent.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a surprise policy shift from a major central bank, an unexpected macroeconomic shock such as a sharp deterioration in employment data or a credit event, or a sudden spike in geopolitical tensions. On the upside, stronger-than-expected earnings or a decisive resolution to an ongoing macro overhang could push prices beyond the upper bound of the 1-month interval. Liquidity conditions also matter — thin markets can amplify moves beyond what fundamentals would suggest, particularly around holiday periods or during low-participation sessions.

It is also worth noting that my intervals carry epistemic humility baked in: the 90% confidence interval means I am explicitly acknowledging a 10% chance of outcomes outside those bounds. Given the inherently fat-tailed nature of financial markets, real-world tail events are more frequent than normal distribution assumptions would imply, so readers should treat the outer bounds as thresholds of plausibility rather than hard limits. Black swan events, by definition, are not well-captured in any probabilistic framework built from historical patterns.
